note: Rehearsed assistant exchanges for the pitch. Served when the model is unavailable or in demo mode (?demo=1). Replies quote no computed numbers; the pages show them.

entries.reply: Nobile Rim 2 is one of the nine regions NASA is considering for Artemis III, on the rim of Nobile crater. Little ground around it stands higher, so the Sun and Earth both stay in view for long stretches; Explore's answer gives the numbers for the period you set.

entries.prompt: Compare de Gerlache Rim 2 and Nobile Rim 2 for 14 days
entries.reply: Comparing de Gerlache Rim 2 and Nobile Rim 2 over 14 days. de Gerlache Rim 2 is closer to the pole, where the Sun stays lower and nearby hills hide it more often, so expect longer nights; Nobile Rim 2 is farther from the pole, with a more open view. The table gives each site's sunlight, contact with Earth, longest night and time with power, and the sentence above it names the best site for each.

entries.prompt: Which site should Artemis III pick?
entries.reply: That depends on the landing date and on what the lander needs, which is what Compare sites shows: I have lined up de Gerlache Rim 2, Nobile Rim 2 and Malapert Massif. Read sunlight and the longest night for power, Earth in view for radio contact, and the time with power for how long a solar lander lasts from the first day. Then press "Find the best landing day for these sites in the next 12 months" to move the date.

Searching the next 12 months for the landing date from which a solar lander keeps power longest over 14 days, landing only while the Sun is up; when two dates tie, the one with more contact with Earth wins. The period moves to that date when the search finishes.

entries.prompt: Can the lander survive the night?
entries.reply: Explore's answer says how long a solar lander that lands on the first day keeps power at the selected site, with the panel, load and battery you set, and, if night comes first, when power returns. To see what it takes to keep power for the whole period, press Lander and raise the battery or lower the load.
Load set to 300 W. Explore's answer updates at once: a higher load runs the battery down faster in every hour without sunlight, so power can run out sooner.

Switched to a flat panel facing up. Near the pole the Sun stays low in the sky, so a flat panel collects far less than an upright one that turns to follow the Sun; watch how the time with power changes.
Mast set to 5 m. The hills around the site are worked out again from that height; a taller mast sees over more of the nearby hills, which can add hours of sunlight and of contact with Earth.

The longest night is the longest run of hours in the period when no part of the Sun clears the hills around the site. Near the south pole the Sun circles the horizon at a low angle, so one ridge can cut a lunar day into several short days and nights. A solar lander draws on its battery through each night, which is why the time with power depends on the longest night rather than the average; whether it stays warm enough through the night is a separate question the forecast does not answer.

IM-2 Athena landed on 6 March 2025 near Mons Mouton, tipped onto its side in a cold, shadowed crater, and its batteries ran out within a day, with most of the lunar day still ahead. The period now starts at the landing, so you can see the sunlight it could not use; Accuracy compares the sunsets the app predicts with how real missions ended.

Opening Accuracy: four checks of the app's numbers and one piece of context. The Sun's and Earth's directions against NASA JPL's own calculator, sunlight against NASA's sunlight maps worked out their way, the app's shadows against pictures from NASA's lunar orbiter, and the power sums worked out in your browser; past missions are shown as context, not a check. Three meet their criteria; the shadows check misses its own mark, and the page shows where. Each says what it leaves out, and the first has a button that checks against JPL live.

entries.prompt: Show me the list of landing sites
entries.reply: Opening the site list: every place the app knows near the south pole, sorted by how long a solar lander keeps power there from its best landing day in the period. Pick one to open it in Explore.
